title: Numbers and age
goal: Count from one to a hundred, give your age and phone number, and accept the fact that the first four Icelandic numbers change form with the gender of what's being counted.
bekal: count 1–100 and give prices in króna
choose *einn*, *ein*, or *eitt* according to the gender of the noun that goes with it
ask and answer about age with *hvað ertu gamall / gömul*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Í móttökunni
dialogs.intro: The front desk of the language school. Búdí is signing up for the next course; the clerk fills in the form as she asks questions.

lines.speaker: Starfsmaður:
lines.text: Góðan daginn. Hvað heitir þú fullu nafni?
lines.id: Good afternoon. What's your full name?
lines.literal: good day-the. what are-called you full name?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég er tuttugu og fimm ára.
lines.literal: I am twenty and five years.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Sex — fjórir — tveir — níu — átta — einn — núll.
lines.id: Six, four, two, nine, eight, one, zero.
lines.literal: six four two nine eight one zero.

lines.speaker: Starfsmaður:
lines.text: Gott. Þú ert í hópi tvö. Þið eruð tólf í hópnum.
lines.id: Good. You're in group two. There are twelve of you in the group.
lines.literal: good. you are in group two. you-all are twelve in group-the.

lines.speaker: Starfsmaður:
lines.text: Þrjátíu og fimm þúsund krónur. Þrír tímar á viku.
lines.id: Thirty-five thousand krónur. Three hours a week.
lines.literal: thirty and five thousand krónur. three hours on week.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Fínt. Ein spurning enn: hvenær byrjar það?
lines.id: Fine. One more question: when does it start?
lines.literal: fine. one question more: when begins it?

notes: **Hvað ertu gamall? literally "what are you old?"** — and the word *gamall* follows the gender of the person asked. To a man: *Hvað ertu **gamall**?*; to a woman: *Hvað ertu **gömul**?* Getting it wrong isn't just a grammar slip; it sounds as if you've mistaken who you're talking to.
**Ára never changes.** *Ég er tuttugu og fimm ára*, *hún er þriggja ára*, *hann er níutíu ára* — one form for every age. It's one of the few words in Icelandic that truly stays still.

**The first four numbers change with the noun's gender**, and you can see it twice in this dialogue: *ein spurning* (*spurning* is kvk) but *þrír tímar* (*tími* is kk). From 5 up, numbers never change, so the load is limited — but 1–4 are exactly the numbers you use most.

**House numbers and any number standing on its own use the neuter form**: *þrjátíu og þrjú*, not *þrjátíu og þrír*. Hvorugkyn is the language's default form — the same pattern you saw with adjectives in Unit 3.
**Að eiga heima literally "to own home"**, and it means "to live (somewhere)". It's freely interchangeable with *búa* from Unit 2: *Hvar áttu heima?* = *Hvar býrðu?*

**Krónur sound like a lot, and the numbers are indeed big.** A cup of coffee is about 700 krónur, a course 35,000. Don't be surprised to hear thousands in everyday conversation; that's why *þúsund* is one of the words you'll hear most at the checkout.

grammars.title: Numbers 1–4 change with the gender
body: Four numbers, three forms each. The rest — from five up — never change at all.
after: Since only 1–4 change, learn these twelve forms as one block and leave the rest alone. Those twelve forms cover more than half the numbers you say in a day.

⚠️ When a number stands on its own — counting, giving a number, saying a year — use the **hvorugkyn** form: *einn, tveir, þrír* are used when counting in sequence, but *eitt, tvö, þrjú* for numbers and stand-alone figures. In practice, listen first to how Icelanders count; you'll hear both.

grammars.title: Asking about quantity and price
body: One question word, three forms — again according to the gender of the noun being counted.
after: *Hvað kostar* uses the singular even when asking about several things: *Hvað kosta bækurnar?* with plural *kosta* is also correct and just as common.
To answer about a price, the number alone is enough: *Sjö hundruð krónur* — or even just *sjö hundruð*, since the currency is obvious.

sections.title: Numbers from one to a hundred

blocks.text: Combined numbers always have **og** in the middle: *tuttugu **og** fimm*, *níutíu **og** níu*. There's no short form like English "twenty-five" without "and" — the word *og* is required.

blocks.title: Phone numbers are read digit by digit
items: Icelandic phone numbers have seven digits and are read **one digit at a time**, not in pairs: *sex, fjórir, tveir, níu, átta, einn, núll*.
Dates use ordinal forms you haven't learned yet (*fyrsti*, *annar*, *þriðji*), but in casual conversation ordinary numbers are used too: *þriðja mars* — the third of March.
